source_refs.note: Practice MCQs written from Chapter 12 (PDF 261-279, printed 258-276); not printed in the book. Based on the chapter's text, tables, boxes and worked examples (numericals with changed values); none repeats the chapter exercise. Drafts needing academic review.

blocks.text: Practice MCQs for the whole of Chapter 12 (Nuclear and Particle Physics), arranged by the chapter's sections. Each question has one correct answer with a short explanation; numerical questions show the working.
12.1 Structure and properties of the nucleus

blocks.prompt: 1 Experiments confirmed that particles such as nucleons have even smaller constituents. These constituents were named:
blocks.explanation: Physicists looked for more fundamental constituents, later confirmed by experiments, and named them quarks (12.1).

book_ref.quote: These were named as quarks.

blocks.prompt: 2 The mesons discovered by the end of the 1960s mostly had masses:

options.text: less than nucleon masses but more than the electron mass

blocks.explanation: Those mesons had masses mostly less than nucleon masses but more than the electron mass (12.1).

book_ref.quote: These were called mesons whose masses were mostly less than nucleon masses but more than the electron mass.

blocks.prompt: 3 The nucleus of protium, the simplest hydrogen atom, consists of:
blocks.explanation: A proton is the nucleus of the simplest atom, hydrogen, called protium (12.1).

book_ref.quote: A proton is the nucleus of the simplest atom, hydrogen, called a protium.

blocks.prompt: 4 The charge on a proton is:
blocks.explanation: The proton has a positive charge of the same magnitude as the electron, 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C (12.1).

book_ref.quote: The proton has a positive charge of the same magnitude as that of the electron

blocks.prompt: 5 The mass of a proton is about:
blocks.explanation: The proton's mass is 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg (12.1).

book_ref.quote: its mass is 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg

blocks.prompt: 6 The existence of the neutron was pointed out in 1932 by:
blocks.explanation: The neutron's existence was pointed out in 1932 by James Chadwick (12.1).

book_ref.quote: whose existence was pointed out in 1932 by James Chadwick

blocks.prompt: 7 The protons and neutrons inside a nucleus are together called:
blocks.explanation: The two types of particles in the nucleus, neutrons and protons, are called nucleons (12.1).

book_ref.quote: Now we can say that the nucleus has two types of particles (neutrons and protons) called nucleons.

blocks.prompt: 8 The different nuclei of the elements are called:
blocks.explanation: The different nuclei are called nuclides (12.1).

book_ref.quote: The different nuclei are called nuclides.

blocks.prompt: 9 The atomic number Z of a nucleus is the number of:
blocks.explanation: The number of protons in a nucleus is the atomic number Z (12.1).

book_ref.quote: The number of protons in a nucleus is called the atomic number represented by the symbol Z.

blocks.prompt: 10 A nucleus has mass number A = 40 and atomic number Z = 18. Its neutron number N is:

book_ref.quote: where N represents the neutron number.

blocks.prompt: 11 A nucleus contains 15 protons and 16 neutrons. Its mass number A is:
blocks.explanation: A is the total number of nucleons: A = Z + N = 15 + 16 = 31 (12.1).

book_ref.quote: is represented by the symbol A and is called the atomic mass number

blocks.prompt: 12 One unified mass unit (1 u) is defined as exactly:

options.text: the mass of a hydrogen atom
one twelfth the mass of a carbon-12 atom
one twelfth the mass of a carbon-14 atom

blocks.explanation: By definition 1 u is exactly one twelfth the mass of a carbon-12 atom (12.1).

book_ref.quote: By definition 1u is exactly one twelveth the mass of carbon¹² atom

blocks.prompt: 13 In energy units, 1 u is equivalent to:
blocks.explanation: The chapter gives 1 u = 1.6606 × 10⁻²⁷ kg = 931 MeV (12.1).

book_ref.quote: To indicate the mass of atomic particles, instead of kilogram, unified mass scale (u) is generally used.

blocks.prompt: 14 Using 1 u = 931 MeV, by how much does the rest-mass energy of a neutron (1.008665 u) exceed that of a proton (1.007276 u)?

book_ref.quote: In this unit the mass of a proton is 1.007276 u and that of a neutron is 1.008665 u

blocks.prompt: 15 Taking the proton's mass as 1.007276 u and the electron's as 0.00055 u, the proton is about how many times heavier than the electron?

book_ref.quote: while that of an electron is 0.00055 u

blocks.prompt: 16 Nuclei having the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons are called:
blocks.explanation: Same Z, different N: such nuclei are isotopes (12.1).

book_ref.quote: Nuclei that contain the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons are called isotopes.

blocks.prompt: 17 Which isotope of carbon is unstable and decays into nitrogen?
blocks.explanation: C-12 and C-13 are stable, but C-14 is unstable and decays into nitrogen with emission of β and neutrino particles (12.1).

book_ref.quote: is unstable and decays into nitrogen alongwith the emission of β and neutrino particles

blocks.prompt: 18 How many neutrons are there in the carbon isotope with mass number 13?
blocks.explanation: Carbon always has 6 protons; N = A − Z = 13 − 6 = 7 (12.1).

book_ref.quote: For example, carbon nuclei always have 6 protons, but they may have 6, 7 and 8 neutrons.

blocks.prompt: 19 Which one of the following is NOT one of the four fundamental forces?
blocks.explanation: The four fundamental forces are gravity, electromagnetism, weak nuclear force and strong nuclear force (12.2).

book_ref.quote: The four fundamental forces are gravity, electromagnetism, weak nuclear force, and strong nuclear force.

blocks.prompt: 20 Among the four fundamental forces, gravity is:
blocks.explanation: Gravity is the weakest of the four but it is a long-range force (12.2).

book_ref.quote: It is the weakest of the four but it is a long-range force.

blocks.prompt: 21 Gravitational force between particles on an atomic level is considered:
blocks.explanation: Gravity is significant for massive objects, but on an atomic level it is negligibly weak (12.2).

book_ref.quote: However, on an atomic level, this force is considered to be negligibly weak.

blocks.prompt: 22 Electricity and magnetism were unified into electromagnetism by a set of four equations formulated by:
blocks.explanation: James Clerk Maxwell (1861) formulated four equations that unified electricity and magnetism (12.2).

book_ref.quote: James Clerk Maxwell (1861) formulated a set of four fundamental equations

blocks.prompt: 23 The electromagnetic force resembles the gravitational force in that both:
blocks.explanation: Like gravity, the electromagnetic force follows an inverse square law, but it is much stronger (12.2).

book_ref.quote: Like the gravitational force, the electromagnetic force follows an inverse square law

blocks.prompt: 24 If only the electromagnetic and gravitational forces acted in a nucleus, the nucleus would:
blocks.explanation: With only electromagnetism and gravity, the nucleus should fly off; its stability implies a stronger nuclear force (12.2).

book_ref.quote: If we only consider the forces of electromagnetism and gravity, the nucleus should fly off in different directions.

blocks.prompt: 25 Strong nuclear forces are called short-range forces because they:
blocks.explanation: Strong nuclear forces only exist inside the nucleus, so they are short-range forces (12.2).

book_ref.quote: So, we call them as short-range forces.

blocks.prompt: 26 The strong nuclear force acts as an attractive force between:

options.text: all nucleons, protons and neutrons alike

blocks.explanation: The strong nuclear force attracts all nucleons, protons and neutrons alike (12.2).

book_ref.quote: The strong nuclear force acts as an attractive force between all nucleons, protons and neutrons alike.

blocks.prompt: 27 Two protons inside a nucleus:

options.text: attract via the strong force and repel via the electric force
only attract via the electric force
exert no force on each other

blocks.explanation: Protons attract each other via the strong nuclear force and at the same time repel via the electric force (12.2).

book_ref.quote: Thus, protons attract each other via the strong nuclear force at the same time they repel each other via the electric force.

blocks.prompt: 28 Beta decay is mainly due to the:
blocks.explanation: Weak nuclear forces are responsible for radioactive decay, particularly beta decay (12.2).

book_ref.quote: Weak nuclear forces are responsible for the radioactive decay, particularly the beta decay

blocks.prompt: 29 Which fundamental force can change the identity of particles?
blocks.explanation: Unlike the others, the weak force can change the identity of particles; this is essential for fusion in stars (12.2).

book_ref.quote: Unlike the other fundamental forces, the weak force can change the identity of particles

blocks.prompt: 30 According to Table 12.1, the range of the strong nuclear force is:
blocks.explanation: Table 12.1: strong force range < 10⁻¹⁵ m (12.2).

book_ref.quote: Table 12.1 Relative strength and range of four fundamental forces

blocks.prompt: 31 Which fundamental force has the shortest range (less than 10⁻¹⁸ m)?
blocks.explanation: Table 12.1: weak force range < 10⁻¹⁸ m, shorter than the strong force (< 10⁻¹⁵ m) (12.2).

book_ref.quote: Table 12.1 Relative strength and range of four fundamental forces

blocks.prompt: 32 Which two fundamental forces have infinite range?
blocks.explanation: Table 12.1 gives range ∞ for gravity and the electromagnetic force (12.2).

book_ref.quote: Table 12.1 Relative strength and range of four fundamental forces

blocks.prompt: 33 Using the relative strengths in Table 12.1 (electromagnetic 10⁻², gravity 10⁻³⁸), the electromagnetic force is stronger than gravity by a factor of about:

book_ref.quote: Table 12.1 Relative strength and range of four fundamental forces

blocks.prompt: 34 By Table 12.1, the strong force is stronger than the weak force by a factor of about:
blocks.explanation: Strong = 1, weak = 10⁻¹³, so the ratio is 1/10⁻¹³ = 10¹³ (12.2).

book_ref.quote: Table 12.1 Relative strength and range of four fundamental forces

blocks.prompt: 35 A neutron attracts other nucleons through the:
blocks.explanation: Being electrically neutral, a neutron attracts other neutrons or protons via the strong nuclear force (12.2).

book_ref.quote: A neutron, being electrically neutral, can attract other neutrons or protons via the strong nuclear force.

blocks.prompt: 36 The existence of anti-particles was predicted in 1928 by:
blocks.explanation: Paul Dirac predicted in 1928 that fundamental particles have anti-particles (12.3).

book_ref.quote: It was predicted by Paul Dirac in 1928 that the fundamental particles have their anti-particles.

blocks.prompt: 37 Compared with its particle, an anti-particle has:

options.text: the same rest mass but opposite charge
the same charge but a larger mass
opposite charge and half the mass

blocks.explanation: Anti-particles have the same rest mass as their particles but opposite charge (12.3).

book_ref.quote: The rest masses of the anti-particles are the same as that of their corresponding particles but with opposite charges.

blocks.prompt: 38 Anderson discovered the positron in 1932 in a:
blocks.explanation: The positron was discovered by Anderson in 1932 in a cloud chamber experiment (12.3).

book_ref.quote: by Anderson in 1932 in a cloud chamber experiment

blocks.prompt: 39 An anti-particle is usually represented by:

options.text: a letter with a star on it
a letter with a dot under it
a letter with a bar over it

blocks.explanation: Anti-particles are written with a bar over the letter, e.g. anti-proton p̄, antineutrino ν̄ (12.3).

book_ref.quote: Usually, the anti-particle are represented by a letter with a bar over it

blocks.prompt: 40 The antiproton was discovered in 1955 by:
blocks.explanation: In 1955, Segre and Chamberlain discovered the antiproton using a particle accelerator (12.3).

book_ref.quote: In 1955, Segre and Chamberlain discovered antiproton using a particle accelerator

blocks.prompt: 41 Which one of the following is NOT a particle accelerator?
blocks.explanation: Linear accelerators, cyclotrons and betatrons are particle accelerators; a cloud chamber is where the positron was observed (12.3).

book_ref.quote: Linear Accelerators, Cyclotrons and Betatrons are important particle accelerators.

blocks.prompt: 42 Cosmic rays coming from outer space consist mostly of:
blocks.explanation: Cosmic ray particles consist mostly of protons, neutrons and heavier nuclei (12.3).

book_ref.quote: These particles consist mostly of protons, neutrons and heavier nuclei

blocks.prompt: 43 Among the many discovered particles, the two groups recognized as elementary particles are:
blocks.explanation: Quarks and leptons are recognized as the fundamental (elementary) particles, and they have antiparticles too (12.3).

book_ref.quote: The quarks and leptons have been recognized as the fundamental particles

blocks.prompt: 44 When accelerated charged particles collide head-on, the debris may contain:

options.text: pions, kaons, muons and even antiprotons

blocks.explanation: The debris from such collisions contains pions, kaons, muons and even antiprotons (12.3).

book_ref.quote: the debris from these reactions contain particles like pions, kaons, muons and even antiprotons

blocks.prompt: 45 Pair production takes place when a high-energy gamma ray photon:

options.text: strikes an electron at rest only

blocks.explanation: Pair production occurs when a gamma photon passes near an atomic nucleus, giving an electron-positron pair (12.3).

book_ref.quote: Pair production occurs when a gamma ray photon (high energy photon) passes nearby an atomic nucleus.

blocks.prompt: 46 In pair production, a nucleus is necessary in order to conserve:
blocks.explanation: A third particle such as a nucleus is necessary to conserve linear momentum (12.3).

book_ref.quote: The presence of a third particle, such as a nucleus, is necessary to conserve linear momentum.

blocks.prompt: 47 The minimum photon energy needed to create an electron-positron pair is:
blocks.explanation: The minimum energy equals the pair's rest mass energy, 2m₀c² = 1.02 MeV (12.3).

book_ref.quote: The rest mass energy of the electron-positron pair is 2m₀c² = 1.02 MeV

blocks.prompt: 48 A 1.80 MeV gamma photon produces an electron-positron pair. The total kinetic energy of the pair is:
blocks.explanation: KE = 1.80 − 1.02 = 0.78 MeV; the excess over 1.02 MeV goes into kinetic energy (12.3).

book_ref.quote: the excess energy goes into the kinetic energies of the particles

blocks.prompt: 49 A gamma photon of energy 0.90 MeV passes near a nucleus. What happens?

options.text: A pair is produced with 0.12 MeV kinetic energy

blocks.explanation: 0.90 MeV < 1.02 MeV, so the photon cannot produce an electron-positron pair (12.3).

book_ref.quote: A gamma ray photon with energy less than 1.02 MeV cannot produce an electron-positron pair

blocks.prompt: 50 A 3.02 MeV photon creates an electron-positron pair. If the kinetic energy is shared equally, each particle gets:

book_ref.quote: the excess energy goes into the kinetic energies of the particles

blocks.prompt: 51 Pair production cannot take place:

options.text: in vacuum, away from any nucleus

blocks.explanation: Pair production needs an external object like a nucleus that can recoil; it cannot take place in vacuum (12.3).

book_ref.quote: The pair production cannot take place in vacuum or space.

blocks.prompt: 52 In pair production the total charge before and after the process is:
blocks.explanation: The photon has no charge and the pair has −e + e = 0; pair production conserves charge, momentum and energy (12.3).

book_ref.quote: The process of pair production satisfies the laws of conservation of charge, momentum and energy.

blocks.prompt: 53 Annihilation of matter is the opposite process of:
blocks.explanation: Annihilation is the opposite process of pair production (12.3).

book_ref.quote: It is the opposite process of pair production.

blocks.prompt: 54 When an electron and a positron at rest annihilate, each of the two gamma photons has energy:
blocks.explanation: Each photon has 0.51 MeV, equal to the rest mass energy m₀c² of an electron or a positron (12.3).

book_ref.quote: The energy of each gamma ray photon is 0.51 MeV

blocks.prompt: 55 Using 1 MeV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ J, the total energy released when an electron and a positron at rest annihilate (1.02 MeV) is:
blocks.explanation: E = 1.02 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ = 1.63 × 10⁻¹³ J; energy is conserved in annihilation (12.3).

book_ref.quote: In an annihilation reaction energy and momentum are conserved.

blocks.prompt: 56 Besides electron and positron, annihilation can also occur between:
blocks.explanation: Annihilation of other particles with their anti-particles also occurs, e.g. proton and antiproton, quark and antiquark (12.3).

book_ref.quote: the annihilation reactions of other particles and their anti-particles can also be carried out

blocks.prompt: 57 High energy collisions at CERN have shown that part of the mass of colliding particles changes into:

options.text: electromagnetic radiation, and the left-over mass appears as new particles

blocks.explanation: Some mass changes to electromagnetic radiation by Einstein's equation and the left-over mass appears as new sub-atomic particles (12.3).

book_ref.quote: High energy collisions between the particles at CERN have revealed

blocks.prompt: 58 Nuclei are found naturally unstable (radioactive) when their atomic number is greater than:
blocks.explanation: Nuclei with atomic numbers greater than 82 are naturally unstable and emit radiation spontaneously (12.4).

book_ref.quote: the nuclei whose atomic numbers are greater than 82 are found naturally unstable

blocks.prompt: 59 When a stable element is bombarded with high-energy particles and becomes radioactive, the process is called:
blocks.explanation: Making a stable element unstable by bombardment with neutrons, protons, alpha particles or gamma rays is artificial radioactivity (12.4).

book_ref.quote: This is called artificial radioactivity

blocks.prompt: 60 In an electric field, α-particles bend towards the negative terminal. This shows that they:
blocks.explanation: Deflection towards the negative terminal shows α-particles have positive charge (12.4).

book_ref.quote: α-particles deflect towards the negative terminal of the electric field

blocks.prompt: 61 β-particles are deflected more than α-particles in an electric field because β-particles are:
blocks.explanation: The larger deflection of β-particles proves they are lighter than α-particles (12.4).

book_ref.quote: The deflection of β-particles is more than the α-particles

blocks.prompt: 62 Taking the speed of light as 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, the greatest speed of β-particles stated in the chapter (0.9995 of c) is:

book_ref.quote: move with speeds up to 0.9995 of the speed of light

blocks.prompt: 63 γ-radiations pass through an electric field without deflection, which shows that they:
blocks.explanation: No deflection shows γ-radiations have no charge (12.4).

book_ref.quote: The γ-radiations passed through the electric field without deflection

blocks.prompt: 64 γ-radiations consist of:
blocks.explanation: γ-radiations are electromagnetic radiations consisting of photons, moving with the speed of light (12.4).

book_ref.quote: The γ-radiations are electromagnetic radiations which consist of photons.

blocks.prompt: 65 α-particles travel only several centimetres in air because of their:
blocks.explanation: Due to their large mass, α-particles travel only several centimetres in air (12.4).

book_ref.quote: α-particles can travel only several centimetres in the air due to their large mass

blocks.prompt: 66 α-particles are emitted at speeds that are typically:

options.text: equal to the speed of light
a few percent of the speed of light

blocks.explanation: α-particles are emitted at high speeds, typically a few percent of the speed of light (12.4).

book_ref.quote: typically a few percent of the speed of light

blocks.prompt: 67 An α-particle is equivalent to:

options.text: a helium nucleus (two protons and two neutrons)

blocks.explanation: An α-particle is a helium nucleus with two protons and two neutrons (12.4).

book_ref.quote: An α-particle is equivalent to a helium (He) nucleus which consists of two protons and two neutrons.

blocks.prompt: 68 In α-decay the parent nucleus:

options.text: Z decreases by 2 and A decreases by 4
Z decreases by 4 and A by 2

blocks.explanation: Losing two protons and two neutrons, Z decreases by two and A by four (Eq. 12.2).

book_ref.quote: Hence the atomic number Z decreases by two while its mass number A decreases by four.

blocks.prompt: 69 A nucleus with A = 210 and Z = 84 emits an α-particle. The daughter nucleus has:

book_ref.quote: is the parent nucleus which decays into the daughter nucleus

blocks.prompt: 70 The change of one element into another by radioactive decay is called:
blocks.explanation: The transition of one element into another is the transmutation of elements (12.4).

book_ref.quote: This transition of one element into another is called the transmutation of the elements.

blocks.prompt: 71 In α-decay, which quantities are experimentally found to be conserved?

options.text: Number of nucleons and electric charge

blocks.explanation: In α-decay the number of nucleons (A) and electric charge are conserved (12.4).

book_ref.quote: it is experimentally observed that the number of nucleons (A) and electric charge are conserved

blocks.prompt: 72 In an α-decay the parent is heavier than the daughter plus the α-particle by 0.0060 u. Using 1 u = 931 MeV, the disintegration energy Q is:
blocks.explanation: Q = 0.0060 × 931 = 5.59 MeV; the mass-energy difference is the Q-value (12.4).

book_ref.quote: This difference in mass-energy is called the disintegration energy Q

blocks.prompt: 73 Radium-226 decays by α-emission into:
blocks.explanation: Ra-226 (Z = 88) emits an α-particle and becomes Rn-222 (Z = 86) (Eq. 12.3).

book_ref.quote: emits an alpha particle and decays into a daughter nucleus radon-222

blocks.prompt: 74 β⁻-decay occurs in nuclides whose neutron-to-proton ratio (N/P) is:
blocks.explanation: Nuclides with N/P too large are the source of β⁻-decay (12.4).

book_ref.quote: Some nuclides have neutron-to-proton ratio (N/P) too large and are the source of β⁻-decay.

blocks.prompt: 75 The electrons emitted in β⁻-decay are:

options.text: orbital electrons knocked out of the atom
created within the nucleus at the moment of emission
electrons stored permanently in the nucleus

blocks.explanation: β-particles are not orbital electrons; they are created within the nucleus at the moment of emission (12.4).

book_ref.quote: The β-particles are not the orbital electrons

blocks.prompt: 76 In β⁻-decay, a neutron in the nucleus changes into:

options.text: a proton, a positron and a neutrino
a proton, an electron and an antineutrino

blocks.explanation: In β⁻-decay, n → p + e⁻ + ν̄ (12.4).

book_ref.quote: a neutron in the nucleus decays into a proton and an electron, plus another particle called antineutrino

blocks.prompt: 77 Cobalt-60 (Z = 27) is a β⁻-emitter. The daughter nucleus has:
blocks.explanation: In β⁻-decay A stays the same and the atomic number Z increases by one: A = 60, Z = 28 (12.4).

book_ref.quote: the parent element of atomic number Z is transmuted to another element of atomic number (Z+1)

blocks.prompt: 78 Nuclides with N/P too small for stability decay by emitting:
blocks.explanation: Nuclides with N/P too small decay by emitting a positron (with a neutrino) (12.4).

book_ref.quote: There are also nuclides that have neutron-to-proton ratio (N/P) too small for stability

blocks.prompt: 79 A nucleus with A = 22 and Z = 11 undergoes β⁺-decay. The daughter nucleus has:
blocks.explanation: In β⁺-decay a proton becomes a neutron: A unchanged, Z − 1 = 10 (12.4).

book_ref.quote: a proton in the nucleus decays into a neutron and a positron, plus a neutrino

blocks.prompt: 80 The neutrino was first proposed in 1930, to obey energy conservation in beta decay, by:
blocks.explanation: Wolfgang Pauli proposed the neutrino in 1930 (12.4).

book_ref.quote: The neutrino was first proposed by Wolfgang Pauli in 1930

blocks.prompt: 81 The neutrino was detected in 1953 by Reines and Cowan in a:
blocks.explanation: Reines and Cowan detected the neutrino in a high-power nuclear reactor (12.4).

book_ref.quote: neutrino was detected by F. Reines and C. L. Cowan

blocks.prompt: 82 Neutrinos and antineutrinos are very difficult to observe because they have:

options.text: zero charge and very small mass

blocks.explanation: Both have zero charge and very small mass, so they are very difficult to observe in matter (12.4).

book_ref.quote: Both the neutrino and the anti-neutrino have zero charge and very small mass

blocks.prompt: 83 The decay of neon-19 into fluorine-19 is an example of:
blocks.explanation: Ne-19 (Z = 10) becomes F-19 (Z = 9) by emitting a positron and a neutrino: β⁺-decay (12.4).

book_ref.quote: An example of a decay of Neon into Flourine by emitting positron and neutrino is:

blocks.prompt: 84 When the number of α-particles is plotted against kinetic energy, the graph shows distinct spikes. This shows that α-particles have:
blocks.explanation: Distinct spikes (Fig. 12.5) show that α-particles have discrete energies (12.4).

book_ref.quote: This demonstrates that α-particles have discrete energies.

blocks.prompt: 85 In β-decay, the kinetic energy of the emitted electron or positron:

options.text: may range from zero to a maximum value
is always exactly the maximum value
is the same for every β-particle

blocks.explanation: Energy is shared with the (anti)neutrino in varying proportions, so the β-particle energy ranges from zero to a maximum (12.4).

book_ref.quote: the energy of an electron or a positron may range from zero to a maximum value

blocks.prompt: 86 In a β⁻-decay the energy released is 1.50 MeV. If the electron carries 0.60 MeV, the antineutrino carries:
blocks.explanation: The sum of the two energies stays the same: 1.50 − 0.60 = 0.90 MeV (12.4).

book_ref.quote: The sum of electron (or positron) energy and the anti-neutrino's (or neutrino's) energy

blocks.prompt: 87 When an excited nucleus emits γ-radiation and goes to its ground state, its A and Z:
blocks.explanation: In X* → X + γ the nucleus keeps the same A and Z; only the excited nucleus goes to its ground state (12.4).

book_ref.quote: represents an excited nucleus while

blocks.prompt: 88 According to Table 12.2, a typical source of γ-rays is:
blocks.explanation: Table 12.2: typical sources are radon-222 (α), strontium-94 (β) and cobalt-60 (γ) (12.4).

book_ref.quote: Table 12.2: The summary of nature of alpha, beta and gamma radiations

blocks.prompt: 89 β-particles are absorbed by about:
blocks.explanation: Table 12.2: α by a paper, β by 1-5 mm of Al, γ by 1-10 cm of lead (12.4).

book_ref.quote: Table 12.2: The summary of nature of alpha, beta and gamma radiations

blocks.prompt: 90 To absorb γ-rays, Table 12.2 gives about:
blocks.explanation: γ-rays are absorbed by 1-10 cm of lead sheet (Table 12.2).

book_ref.quote: Table 12.2: The summary of nature of alpha, beta and gamma radiations

blocks.prompt: 91 From Table 12.2, α-particles produce about 10⁴ ion pairs per mm in air and γ-rays about 1. The ionization by α-particles is greater by a factor of about:

book_ref.quote: Table 12.2: The summary of nature of alpha, beta and gamma radiations

blocks.prompt: 92 In Table 12.2, the radiation whose range in air 'obeys inverse square law' is:
blocks.explanation: α has a range of several centimetres, β several metres, while γ-rays obey the inverse square law (Table 12.2).

book_ref.quote: Table 12.2: The summary of nature of alpha, beta and gamma radiations

blocks.prompt: 93 According to Table 12.2, the typical speed of α-particles is about:
blocks.explanation: Table 12.2: α ~10⁷ m s⁻¹, β ~1 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, γ ~3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ (12.4).

book_ref.quote: Table 12.2: The summary of nature of alpha, beta and gamma radiations

blocks.prompt: 94 A fundamental particle is one that:

options.text: has no internal structure and is indivisible

blocks.explanation: A fundamental particle has no internal structure, i.e. it is indivisible (12.5).

book_ref.quote: a particle that has no internal structure, which means it is indivisible

blocks.prompt: 95 Strange particles are always created:
blocks.explanation: Strange particles are always created in pairs, e.g. k⁰ and Λ⁰ from π⁻ + p (12.5).

book_ref.quote: They are always created in pairs

blocks.prompt: 96 When a pion (π⁻) collides with a proton, the two strange particles created are:

book_ref.quote: two strange particles k⁰ and Λ⁰ are created

blocks.prompt: 97 The spin of a photon is:
blocks.explanation: The spin of the photon is 1; that of electrons, protons and neutrons is 1/2 and of pions zero (12.5).

book_ref.quote: the spin of photon is 1 and of pions is taken as zero

blocks.prompt: 98 Particles with half spin, which obey Pauli's exclusion principle, are called:
blocks.explanation: Half-spin particles obey Pauli's exclusion principle and are called fermions (12.5).

book_ref.quote: Half spin particles obey the Pauli's exclusion principle

blocks.prompt: 99 Particles with zero or whole-number spin are called bosons because they:
blocks.explanation: Particles with zero or whole-number spin do not obey Pauli's principle; they obey Bose-Einstein statistics and are bosons (12.5).

book_ref.quote: as they obey Bose-Einstein statistics

blocks.prompt: 100 The spin of charged particles makes them:
blocks.explanation: All particles spin on their axes; the spin of charged particles makes them tiny magnets (12.5).

book_ref.quote: the spin of charged particles makes them tiny magnets

blocks.prompt: 101 Both β⁻ and β⁺ decay processes provide evidence that:

options.text: protons and neutrons are not fundamental particles

blocks.explanation: β-decay processes provide evidence that protons and neutrons are not fundamental particles (12.5).

book_ref.quote: Both of the β-decay (beta-minus and beta-plus) processes provide evidence

blocks.prompt: 102 The strongly attractive mesons are called:
blocks.explanation: Strongly attractive particles are π mesons (pions); weakly interacting ones were named μ mesons (muons) (12.5).

book_ref.quote: The strongly attractive particles are called π meson or pions

blocks.prompt: 103 Particles that experience the strong force are known as:
blocks.explanation: Particles that interact via the strong force are hadrons; those that do not are leptons (12.5).

book_ref.quote: Those that experience the strong force are known as hadrons

blocks.prompt: 104 Which one of the following is a lepton?
blocks.explanation: Protons, neutrons and pions are hadrons; electrons and neutrinos are leptons (12.5).

book_ref.quote: Examples of hadrons include protons, neutrons, and pions

blocks.prompt: 105 Hadrons that are fermions, such as protons and neutrons, are called:
blocks.explanation: Hadrons divide into bosons (mesons, e.g. pion) and fermions (baryons, e.g. protons and neutrons) (12.5).

book_ref.quote: while others are fermions, known as baryons

blocks.prompt: 106 A meson is usually made up of:
blocks.explanation: Mesons are made of an even number of quarks, usually one quark and one antiquark (12.5).

book_ref.quote: usually two quarks: one quark and one antiquark

blocks.prompt: 107 Leptons interact only through:
blocks.explanation: Leptons interact only through weak or electromagnetic interactions (12.5).

book_ref.quote: The leptons interact only through weak or electromagnetic interactions.

blocks.prompt: 108 All known leptons are fermions because they have spin:
blocks.explanation: All known leptons have spin ½, so they are fermions (12.5).

book_ref.quote: All known leptons have spin ½, so they all are fermions.

blocks.prompt: 109 How many leptons are known (not counting antiparticles)?
blocks.explanation: The six known leptons are grouped as three pairs: e, μ, τ, each with its neutrino (Table 12.3).

book_ref.quote: The six known leptons are grouped as three pairs of particles

blocks.prompt: 110 Using Table 12.3 (muon 105.7 MeV/c², electron 0.511 MeV/c²), the muon is about how many times heavier than the electron?

book_ref.quote: Table 12.3: The lepton family

blocks.explanation: 1777/931 = 1.91 u, almost twice the proton's mass (Table 12.3, 12.1).

book_ref.quote: Table 12.3: The lepton family

blocks.prompt: 112 Neutrinos are rarely observed because they:
blocks.explanation: Neutrinos rarely interact with anything and are consequently rarely observed; the best-known lepton is the electron (12.5).

book_ref.quote: The best-known of all leptons is the electron.

blocks.prompt: 113 In terms of quarks, β⁻-decay of a neutron (udd) into a proton (uud) happens by:

options.text: an up quark changing into a down quark
a down quark changing into an up quark

blocks.explanation: udd → uud by changing a down quark into an up quark: d → u + e⁻ + ν̄ (12.6).

book_ref.quote: by changing a down quark into an up quark

blocks.prompt: 114 The idea that hadrons are made of quarks was proposed in 1964 by:
blocks.explanation: In 1964 Gell-Mann and Zweig proposed that hadrons are made of quarks (12.6).

book_ref.quote: In 1964, M. Gell-Mann and George Zweig proposed

blocks.prompt: 115 The three quarks originally proposed were:
blocks.explanation: The original three quarks were up, down and strange (u, d, s); charm, bottom and top came later (12.6).

book_ref.quote: Three quarks originally proposed were named up, down, and strange

blocks.prompt: 116 How many quark flavours are presently known?
blocks.explanation: Six quarks are known, just as there are six leptons (12.6).

book_ref.quote: Presently, we are aware of six quarks

blocks.prompt: 117 The electric charge of a quark is:

options.text: a fraction of the electron's charge e
a whole-number multiple of e greater than 1

blocks.explanation: All quarks have a charge that is a fraction of e, e.g. +2/3 or −1/3 (12.6).

book_ref.quote: All quarks have a spin and an electric charge

blocks.prompt: 118 According to Table 12.4, the charge of a strange quark is:
blocks.explanation: Table 12.4: s has charge −1/3 (like d and b) (12.6).

blocks.explanation: Table 12.4: top 175000 MeV/c² is far heavier than bottom 4300, charm 1500 and strange 200 MeV/c² (12.6).

book_ref.quote: These new quarks can be distinguished from the 3 original quarks

options.text: an up quark and an anti-down quark
an up quark and a down quark
two up quarks and a down quark
an anti-up quark and a down quark

blocks.prompt: 126 Each flavour of quark can carry one of three 'colours', usually called:
blocks.explanation: Each flavour can have one of three colours, red, green and blue; the names have nothing to do with our senses (12.6).

book_ref.quote: each flavour of quark can have one of three colours

blocks.prompt: 127 The theory of the strong force acting between colour charges is called:
blocks.explanation: The strong force between colour charges is described by quantum chromodynamics (QCD) (12.6).

book_ref.quote: This theory of the strong force is called quantum chromodynamics or QCD

blocks.prompt: 128 A baryon contains one quark of each colour. As a whole, a baryon is:
blocks.explanation: Red + green + blue gives colourless (white); mesons are also colourless (12.6).

book_ref.quote: Both baryons and mesons are thus colourless or white.

blocks.prompt: 129 Which statement about quarks is correct?

options.text: They never appear on their own

blocks.explanation: Quarks are invisible and never appear on their own (12.6).

book_ref.quote: They never appear on their own.

blocks.prompt: 130 Electromagnetic interactions between charged particles occur by the exchange of:
blocks.explanation: Photons carry the electromagnetic force between charged particles (12.7).

book_ref.quote: electromagnetic interactions occur when two positively charged particles send and receive (exchange) photons

blocks.prompt: 131 The carriers of the weak nuclear force are:
blocks.explanation: W⁺, W⁻ and Z bosons carry the weak nuclear force (12.7).

book_ref.quote: the W⁺, W⁻ and Z are the bosons that are the carriers of weak nuclear force

blocks.prompt: 132 The carriers of the gravitational force are:
blocks.explanation: Gravitons are the carriers of the gravitational force (12.7).

book_ref.quote: gravitons are the carriers of gravitational force

blocks.prompt: 133 The Higgs boson was discovered in 2012 at:

options.text: the large hadron collider at CERN

blocks.explanation: The Higgs boson was discovered in 2012 at the large hadron collider at CERN (12.7).

book_ref.quote: The Higgs boson is a special particle discovered in 2012 at large hadron collider at CERN.

blocks.prompt: 134 The mass of the Higgs boson is around:
blocks.explanation: The Higgs boson has a mass of around 125 GeV and decays rapidly into other particles (12.7).

book_ref.quote: Higgs boson has a mass of around 125 giga-electron-volts (GeV)

blocks.prompt: 135 Using 1 u = 931 MeV, the Higgs boson's mass of 125 GeV is about:

book_ref.quote: Higgs boson has a mass of around 125 giga-electron-volts (GeV)

blocks.prompt: 136 Photons have zero rest mass because they:

options.text: interact strongly with the Higgs field
do not interact with the Higgs field
are carriers of the weak force

blocks.explanation: Particles that interact strongly with the Higgs field get more mass; photons do not interact with it, so their rest mass is zero (12.7).

book_ref.quote: the particles like photons do not interact with Higgs field

blocks.prompt: 137 Which particles get more mass by interacting strongly with the Higgs field?
blocks.explanation: Carriers of the electroweak interaction, W⁺, W⁻ and Z, interact strongly with the Higgs field and get more mass (12.7).

book_ref.quote: The particles that interact strongly with Higgs field get more mass

blocks.prompt: 138 Which one of the following is NOT conserved in all nuclear reactions and decays?
blocks.explanation: Energy, momentum, charge, nucleon number, baryon number and lepton number are conserved; the neutron number changes, e.g. in β-decay (12.8).

book_ref.quote: All nuclear process such as nuclear reactions and nuclear decays obey conservation laws such as:

book_ref.quote: All nuclear process such as nuclear reactions and nuclear decays obey conservation laws such as:

blocks.prompt: 140 According to the chapter's classification box, which one of the following is a baryon?
blocks.explanation: Baryons: protons, neutrons, omega, sigma and lambda; pions and kaons are mesons; muons are leptons (12.8).

book_ref.quote: Hadrons Mesons, e.g. pions, kaons baryons

blocks.explanation: Non-hadrons include leptons (electrons, muons, neutrinos), photons and gravitons (12.8).

book_ref.quote: Hadrons Mesons, e.g. pions, kaons baryons

blocks.text: 12.9 The asymmetry of matter and antimatter in the universe

blocks.prompt: 142 Observations show that our universe consists almost entirely of:

options.text: equal amounts of matter and antimatter

blocks.explanation: There is an asymmetry: the universe consists almost entirely of matter rather than antimatter (12.9).

book_ref.quote: the universe consists almost entirely of matter rather than antimatter

blocks.prompt: 143 In the composition of the universe, the contribution of antihydrogen or anti-helium atoms is:
blocks.explanation: There is no contribution of antihydrogen or anti-helium atoms in the composition of the universe (12.9).

book_ref.quote: there are no any contribution of antihydrogen or anti-helium atoms

blocks.prompt: 144 The problem of the asymmetry of matter and antimatter is, according to the chapter:
blocks.explanation: The chapter concludes that the asymmetry of matter and antimatter is still a mystery (12.9).

book_ref.quote: Hence, it is concluded that the problem asymmetry of matter and antimatter is still mystery.

blocks.text: 12.10 Most of the matter in the observable universe is plasma

blocks.prompt: 145 The unknown matter that makes up about 27% of the universe is called:
blocks.explanation: About 27% of the universe is unknown matter called dark matter (12.10).

book_ref.quote: our universe consists of about 27% of unknown matter called dark matter

blocks.prompt: 146 Dark energy makes up about what percentage of the universe?
blocks.explanation: About 68% of the universe is a mysterious antigravity material, dark energy (12.10).

book_ref.quote: about 68% a mysterious antigravity material known as dark energy

blocks.prompt: 147 Dark matter (27%) and dark energy (68%) together make up what part of the universe that we know nothing about?
blocks.explanation: 27% + 68% = 95%; we know about only 5% of the universe (12.10).

book_ref.quote: It means 95% universe is out of our thinking

blocks.prompt: 148 Most of the matter in the observable universe is in the:
blocks.explanation: Hydrogen and helium are almost in the plasma state, so most of the matter in the observable universe is plasma (12.10).

book_ref.quote: Hence, it is concluded that most of the matter in the observable universe is plasma.

blocks.text: 12.11 The theories about the forces between the masses of particles

blocks.prompt: 149 The two theories mentioned to explain the interactions between particles through mediators are:

options.text: quantum field theory and string theory

blocks.explanation: Interactions through mediators are explained by the quantum field theory and the string theory (12.11).

book_ref.quote: we have the following two theories, the quantum field theory and the string theory

blocks.prompt: 150 In quantum field theory, the quanta that exchange momentum and energy between particles are called:
blocks.explanation: The quanta that exchange momentum and energy in the field are called field particles (12.11).

book_ref.quote: are called field particles

blocks.prompt: 151 In quantum field theory, the field particles that mediate interactions are all:
blocks.explanation: Interactions are described by the exchange of field particles (quanta), which are all bosons (12.11).

book_ref.quote: the exchange of field particle or quanta which are all bosons

blocks.prompt: 152 In quantum field theory, the electromagnetic force is mediated by:
blocks.explanation: Photons, the quanta of the electromagnetic field, mediate the electromagnetic force (12.11).

book_ref.quote: the electromagnetic force is mediated by photons called quanta of the electromagnetic field

blocks.prompt: 153 According to string theory, the fundamental particles are:
blocks.explanation: String theory proposes that fundamental particles are tiny vibrating strings instead of points (12.11).

book_ref.quote: are actually tiny vibrating strings

blocks.prompt: 154 In string theory, the properties of a particle, such as mass, are determined by:
blocks.explanation: The strings can be open or closed loops, and their vibrations determine the particle's properties, including mass and force (12.11).

book_ref.quote: their vibrations determine the properties of particles

blocks.prompt: 155 String theory, a possible 'theory of everything', is at present:

options.text: the same as the Standard Model

blocks.explanation: String theory still remains unproved experimentally (12.11).

book_ref.quote: still remains unproved experimentally

blocks.prompt: 156 The standard model is:

options.text: a model of the atom with orbits only
the collection of theories describing the smallest observed particles of matter and their interactions

blocks.explanation: The standard model is the collection of theories that describe the smallest experimentally observed particles and the interaction between energy and matter (12.12).

book_ref.quote: The standard model is the collection of theories

blocks.prompt: 157 In the standard model, matter (only 5% of the universe) is composed of:
blocks.explanation: Matter is composed of quarks and leptons (12.12).

book_ref.quote: Matter, which makes up only 5% of the universe is composed of quarks and leptons.

blocks.prompt: 158 Which force is NOT provided by the fundamental bosons of the standard model?
blocks.explanation: The fundamental bosons provide electromagnetism, the strong and the weak nuclear force; gravity is one thing the model cannot explain (12.12).

book_ref.quote: The fundamental bosons provide three forces

blocks.prompt: 159 The standard model is considered incomplete because it cannot explain:

options.text: gravity, dark matter and dark energy

blocks.explanation: The model is unable to explain gravity, dark matter (27%) and dark energy (68%) (12.12).

book_ref.quote: This model is still considered incomplete.
